newsitem.title: GERMANY: Political rivals pour scorn on SPD's training levy.
newsitem.headline: Political rivals pour scorn on SPD's training levy.

text.p: Germany's coalition parties on Tuesday poured scorn on a plan by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to slap a levy on employers who fail to provide their share of training places for school-leavers.

An extraordinary party conference on youth issues passed the motion after a heated debate on Monday despite opposition from some of the party's leading economic experts, making the levy official policy if the SPD comes to power in 1998.

"This is a further burden on labour as an economic factor," said Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt of the centrist Free Democrats (FDP), junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition. "It will produce fewer training places and make labour in Germany more expensive."

Rexrodt told Berlin's Info Radio the move would push firms to buy their way out of training, abandoning a long-standing consensus system which has been a pillar of Germany's economic success and shifting responsibility more and more to the state.
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) were similarly scathing in a statement released on Monday.

"What we need is to cut labour costs to make German firms more internationally competitive, not raise them," said CDU general secretary Peter Hintze, saying the SPD had proved its fixation on state intervention.
"State allocation of labour doesn't work, 40 years of east German socialism proved that," he added.

The SPD's youth wing had won the support of the party's parliamentary leader and former chairman Rudolf Scharping for the levy, arguing that the number of training places was falling while the number of school-leavers was rising steadily.
They said large firms were shirking their responsibilities, leaving 110,000 school-leavers without a training place this year, and this proved the voluntary system had failed.
